newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK handover advisers in Beijing talks told to quit.
newsitem.headline: HK handover advisers in Beijing talks told to quit.

text.p: China's selected advisers on the Hong Kong handover opened two-day talks in Beijing on Thursday amid growing demands to halt their activities and give the territory's future government a free rein.
The advisers belong to a group known as the Preparatory Committee, of 150 hand-picked Chinese and Hong Kong worthies, chaired by Foreign Minister Qian Qichen.
They are expected to set a framework for future election laws once Hong Kong becomes a quasi-autonomous part of China.
Britain hands Hong Kong back in just 40 days after a century and a half of colonial rule and authorities are racing to iron out unsettled issues to ensure a smooth transition.
Part of the problem lies in the rocky state of Sino-British relations in the 13 years since Hong Kong's fate was sealed.
Hostility, which reached a low point over mild democratic reforms introduced by the last governor Chris Patten, slowed progress to a snail's pace in the mid-1990s.
The two-day plenum in the Chinese capital, the last before the July 1 transition, will concentrate on sovereignty issues.
Separately, experts from both sides are charting administrative details in a Sino-British Joint Liaison Group (JLG).
They will meet here on May 28-30 to discuss the handover ceremony, among major outstanding issues.
Hong Kong politicans have urged the Preparatory Committee to leave a loose framework on future elections to let the incoming government settle details.
The committee, formed to steer Hong Kong through its transition, has acted mainly to arrange a selection of Hong Kong's future leadership.
That task was completed in December when former shipping magnate Tung Chee-hwa was anointed to step into outgoing British governor Chris Patten's shoes.
Tung, who is a vice chairman of the committee, has added his voice to the chorus urging it be wound up as soon as possible.
This would demonstrate that China plans to respect a promise to allow Hong Kong people, and not Beijing's cadres, to run the territory of 6.4 million people.
"There is, clearly, no reason for continued existence of the Preparatory Committee," the Hong Kong Standard newspaper said in an editorial on Thursday.
Some committee members want it to continue long enough to oversee Hong Kong's first post-colonial elections in 1998 and the daily accused the group of seeking desperately to retain power.
"Dissolution of the Committee will reduce them to anonomity," the Standard said.
Foreign Minister Qian told Hong Kong reporters in Beijing on Wednesday that the committee would not be dissolved at the handover, leaving uncertainty over its future activities.
"It will stop working at the right time," he said, sparking speculation the committee would remain in existence but become dormant.
Meanwhile, the upcoming meeting of experts in the JLG plans to tackle the status of Hong Kong's international aviation agreements, extradition treaties and the transfer of government files.
The JLG, made up of senior Chinese and British diplomats, was established over 13 years ago and is due to serve until 2000 to monitor the transition.
Some Chinese officials argue the British should have no role after the handover at midnight on June 30 but the JLG's continuing role was set out in agreed guidelines known as the Joint Declaration.
On the agenda is the wording of the oath to be taken when Hong Kong's new leader, Tung Chee-hwa, and his administration are sworn into office on July 1.
